The dots are laid out on straight radial spokes that all emanate from one shared center, so together they trace a star-burst of spokes: dots along the same spoke are very close in direction, while consecutive spokes are separated by a much larger empty angular gap. worlds.title: Compass needle heading
worlds.headline: Where does the solid triangle point?
worlds.question: This image shows a compass dial. The rim circle, the four long tick marks, the four short diagonal marks and the letter N are fixed decoration: they are drawn in exactly the same place in every image of this set, so they never indicate the answer. The needle is the two-triangle arrow through the centre of the dial. Exactly one of its two triangles is filled with a solid colour; the mirror-image triangle on the other side is only a grey outline. Report the direction that the SOLID coloured triangle points, using the image itself and not what a compass normally does. If it points between two of the four long ticks, round to the nearer one; the four short diagonal marks show the exact halfway lines. Answer with exactly one word: up, right, down, or left.
steps: Keep the coloured pixels
Keep the largest connected region: the solid triangle
Centroid to apex gives the bearing
worlds.final: Round the bearing to the nearest of up, right, down, left

worlds.title: State machine tape run
worlds.headline: Run the tape through the table
worlds.question: The picture shows a transition table, a marker and a tape. Down the left of the table are four coloured circles: these are the four states, one per table row, and no two of them share a colour. Along the top of the table are three coloured squares: these are the three input symbols, one per table column, and no two of them share a colour. Every cell of the table holds a square painted in one of the four state colours: that cell says which state you move to if you are currently in the state of that cell's row and you read the symbol of that cell's column. A cell painted in its own row's colour means you stay where you are. To the left of the circles is a black ring: the marker starts in the state whose circle centre is nearest to the centre of that black ring. Below the table is a tape of coloured squares, each painted in one of the three symbol colours. The tape is read one square at a time from left to right, in the direction of the arrow drawn beneath it, and each square is one step: look up the row of the state you are currently in and the column whose header square has that tape square's colour, and move to the state named by that cell. Nothing about the run is drawn: the path of the marker and the state it ends in appear nowhere in the picture. After every tape square has been read in order, which state is the marker in? Answer with the colour of that state: red, blue, green or orange.
steps: Assign each pixel to its nearest reference colour
One colour at a time (red shown): its state disc and table cells
worlds.final: Rebuild the table from cell positions, then replay the tape

worlds.title: Oneway reachable tank
worlds.headline: Follow the one-way lanes
worlds.question: This picture shows a one-way lane network. Every disc is a junction and every straight gray bar is a lane joining the two junctions at its ends. Each lane carries exactly one black arrowhead at its middle, and that arrowhead points along the only direction in which that lane may be travelled. You start at the green junction. You may move only along lanes, and on each lane only the way its arrowhead points; you may pass through any number of junctions on the way and you may never move against an arrowhead. Three junctions are colored tanks: one blue, one orange and one purple; all other junctions are gray. Lanes join all of these junctions when the arrowheads are ignored, so how near a tank sits to the green junction on the page, how many lanes touch it, and where it lies do not matter; only travel that follows the arrowheads counts. Exactly one of the three tanks can be reached from the green junction under this rule. Which colored tank can be reached from the green junction? Answer blue, orange, or purple.
steps: Find junction discs by their exact colour (gray shown)
Keep lane and arrowhead pixels
worlds.final: Orient each lane by its arrowhead, then search from the green junction

worlds.title: Pipe fewer corners
worlds.headline: Which pipe turns fewer times?
worlds.question: This picture contains exactly two gray pipes. The two pipes never touch each other, and no pipe ever touches or crosses itself. Each pipe runs from one end sitting inside a black ring to its other end, which is covered by a colored square: one pipe ends at the orange square and the other pipe ends at the purple square. Every pipe is built only from horizontal and vertical straight sections, so every bend in a pipe is a right-angle turn. Follow each pipe from its black ring to its colored square and count the right-angle turns you pass along that pipe. How long the pipes are, how much of the picture they cover, and where they sit do not matter; only the number of right-angle turns counts. Which colored square is at the end of the pipe with fewer right-angle turns? Answer orange or purple.
steps: Keep the mid-gray, unsaturated pipe pixels
Keep the saturated pixels: the two end squares
Count each pipe's long straight runs, minus one
worlds.final: Name each pipe by its nearest square; the purple pipe turns fewer times

steps: Find markers by colour (green start ring shown)
Keep the dark route and its centre line
Link markers along the route; at crossovers take the 0° spoke
